hero.title: Flavor Ingredient Search and Substitute Screening from Predicted Odor Descriptors
hero.intro: Flavorists choose from thousands of ingredient molecules: for a client brief they look for ingredients with the target flavor, and when an ingredient is restricted or unavailable they look for one that smells similar. This tool does both with odor profiles predicted by the odor model: search ingredients by target flavor, or find substitutes for a molecule.

a.score_note: Score = weighted geometric mean of the predicted probabilities of the wanted descriptors × weighted geometric mean of (1 − predicted probability) of the unwanted descriptors; with no unwanted descriptors the second factor is 1. Weights: high 1, medium 0.5, low 0.25. The score runs from 0 to 1 and is shown on the page as 0 to 100. How high the predicted probabilities go depends on the descriptor: for milky, creamy and buttery the highest are only 34%, 53% and 64%, so with two or three such descriptors a score of 30 to 40 is already a good match; common descriptors such as fruity and green can score much higher. The score is for comparison, not a pass mark.
a.score_why: A geometric mean is used instead of a sum for two reasons. First, all requirements must be met together: one wanted descriptor with a low probability, or one unwanted descriptor with a high probability, pulls the score down markedly, and the other descriptors cannot make up for it. Second, scores can be compared between searches: the score does not depend on how many descriptors are chosen and does not rise when more are added; the more requirements there are, the harder they are to meet together and the lower the top score. The score is for ranking and comparison only and is not a probability in the strict sense: the predicted probabilities of different descriptors are not independent, and a geometric mean is not a rule for combining probabilities, so the score should not be read as "the probability that the molecule has all these odors". With a single wanted descriptor the score equals its predicted probability, so the ranking is the same as the per-descriptor ranking evaluated below.

results.intro: Both modes are evaluated on the odor predictor's scaffold-split test set ({n} labelled molecules), computed once at the end; the odor-similarity method was chosen beforehand on the validation set only.
results.a_title: Search by brief: precision of the top 10 / 50
results.a_text: For each descriptor, test molecules are ranked by predicted probability; precision@10 / @50 is the share of the top 10 / 50 that are labelled with that descriptor, averaged over 138 descriptors.
results.a_take: The model's top molecules are far better than random, but about the same as a simple fingerprint + logistic regression, with no advantage. A likely reason: ranking for one descriptor depends mostly on a few typical substructures (lactone rings, sulfur atoms), which fingerprints also capture.
results.b_title: Substitutes: true odor overlap of the nearest molecules
results.b_text: For each test molecule, the 10 most similar molecules are found and the mean overlap of their true odor labels with the query's is computed (Jaccard, 0 to 1, higher = more alike). Three ways are compared: by predicted odor profile (this page's "odor similarity"), by structure (Tanimoto), and at random.
results.b_take: Molecules found by predicted odor profile share clearly more odor labels with the query than those found by structure (95% CI of the difference {lo} to {hi}), and are better for {share}% of queries. The mean overlap is only about {mean}, so treat the results as a shortlist. The gain is larger for acyclic molecules, but these were split one by one at random, so homologues can sit in both training and test sets and this part may be optimistic.
limits.1: Based on predicted odor categories; says nothing about odor intensity, thresholds or actual sensory performance.
limits.2: Stability, solubility, cost and availability are not considered.
limits.3: Safety and regulatory compliance of any substitute must be checked separately; regional regulatory status is not shown, so check the official texts.
limits.4: Results are a shortlist that needs a flavorist's judgment and sensory testing.
footer.data: Data and acknowledgements: the odor model was trained on data from The Good Scents Company and Leffingwell & Associates (Sanchez-Lengeling et al., 2019, arXiv:1910.10685, CC BY-NC), curated and merged by OpenPOM (Barsainyan et al., 2023); the raw odor labels are not redistributed here and the page shows model predictions only. The model and its predictions are for non-commercial academic demonstration only.
footer.kb: Natural occurrence: from this site's flavor knowledge base, derived from FlavorDB2 (Garg et al., NAR 2018, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0). Names: flavor knowledge base or PubChem.
b.intro: Molecules that smell alike but differ in structure may avoid the original's regulatory, patent or supply issues.
bg.diacetyl: Diacetyl itself is a permitted food flavoring. The concern is occupational inhalation in production settings: workers in flavoring and microwave popcorn production who breathed diacetyl vapor over time have developed a serious lung disease (bronchiolitis obliterans). It is not a food-safety issue. In 2016 the US National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH) recommended exposure limits of 5 ppb as an 8-hour time-weighted average and 25 ppb for 15 minutes; these are recommendations, not enforceable OSHA standards. That is why manufacturers look for substitutes.
src.diacetyl: Sources: NIOSH (2016). Criteria for a Recommended Standard: Occupational Exposure to Diacetyl and 2,3-Pentanedione. DHHS (NIOSH) Publication No. 2016-111; OSHA, Flavorings-Related Lung Disease.
bg.coumarin: EU: Regulation (EC) No 1334/2008 on flavourings, Annex III Part A: coumarin (1,2-benzopyrone) shall not be added as such to food; Part B: in compound foods to which flavourings or food ingredients with flavouring properties (such as cinnamon) have been added, coumarin naturally present may not exceed 50 mg/kg in traditional and/or seasonal bakery ware with a reference to cinnamon in the labelling, 20 mg/kg in breakfast cereals including muesli, 15 mg/kg in other fine bakery ware and 5 mg/kg in desserts; the limits do not apply when only fresh, dried or frozen herbs and spices, and no flavourings, have been added. US: under 21 CFR 189.130, food containing added coumarin, as such or as a constituent of tonka beans or tonka extract, is deemed adulterated.
src.coumarin: Sources: Regulation (EC) No 1334/2008, Official Journal of the European Union L 354, 31.12.2008, p. 34, Annex III; 21 CFR 189.130. Regulatory information is for reference only; the latest official texts prevail.
bg.vanillin: Natural vanillin comes from vanilla pods and the yield is low: about 500 kg of pods give 1 kg of vanillin, a slow, laborious and costly process. Less than 1% of the world's vanillin comes from the vanilla orchid; the rest is mostly made by chemical synthesis or from lignin.
src.vanillin: Source: Gallage NJ, et al. Vanillin formation from ferulic acid in Vanilla planifolia is catalysed by a single enzyme. Nature Communications 2014, 5:4037. doi:10.1038/ncomms5037.

hero.sub: Search 5,000+ molecules by target flavor, or find substitutes that smell alike.
a.score_short: Score (0–100) = geometric mean of the wanted descriptors’ probabilities × geometric mean of (1 − probability) for the unwanted ones. A molecule scores high only if it has all the wanted notes.
b.intro_short: Pick a molecule: the 20 most similar in predicted odor; orange ones differ in structure.
about.b_method: Odor similarity is the cosine similarity of two molecules' predicted probabilities for 138 descriptors (chosen on the validation split); structure similarity is the Tanimoto coefficient of their Morgan fingerprints (radius 2, 2048 bits). The scatter plot shows both for every library molecule against the query.
footer.short: Results are a shortlist. No regulatory status is shown here; check safety and compliance separately. The odor model is CC BY-NC, non-commercial academic demo only. See method & sources.
about.practice: Finding candidate compounds for a given flavor usually takes time. For natural-leaning needs, I search the literature with the food name plus flavor compounds as keywords; for a flavor not tied to any food, it means reading a large amount of literature. AI can help, but in my experience it mostly returns the few dozen common compounds and rarely covers the full range. This tool searches 5,000+ molecules by predicted odor descriptors to widen the candidate list first, before people screen it. When looking for a substitute, regulation is usually the main concern after flavor. This page does not show regulatory status, so it must be checked separately.
